doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

chapter: Civil rights era and his mother's example
title: Music reflecting the times; Evers, King and civil rights visitors in Jackson
summary: Rowe quotes Rashied Ali on music reflecting the times; Griffin recalls the assassinations, seeing celebrities and freedom riders in Jackson, his mother feeding them, and neighbors' charity.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I asked Rashied Ali, I was trying to understand the motivation or the inspiration for playing what — I’ll use your term, avant garde and I wondered if he, with his fellow musicians sat down and had a conversation about making the music more exploratory or adventurous. Did you talk about it? And he said no. We didn’t ever talk about it. We just did it. But he went on to say that the music that they were doing was a reflection of the times. And he related some of the segregation things he had experienced, and he said, now I’m going to quote him, “We are not the same people that lived in the bebop era. We live in a different age and I think that’s evolution. Everything changes over time and the music reflects the way you live.”

Yes. That’s right. Okay. Good example: When I was in Indiana University in 1965 to 1967 I was always — well my friend Medgar Evers had been killed and President Kennedy had been killed, and I was in a recording session and my dear friend Dr. Martin

Luther King was killed. I was in a recording session. And Dr. King — and when I was in Jackson, I was eating lunch with Medgar Evers, Dr. King was eating lunch next door in a place called the College Inn, and he had a lot of celebrities like Harry Belafonte, Lena Horne, Sammy Davis Junior, James Baldwin, I saw all of those people in Jackson, when they came through Jackson. And I remember one time there was six of them all there in this place College Inn, and those people that I named, Harry Belafonte, you know, Lena Horne, and there was a lot, Sammy Davis Junior was there that time, and it was just a different time. Stokely Carmichael — we were the same age. I was there, he came through Jackson and SNCC, the group that he was involved — I used to play — I was playing at this place called Junior’s Steak House. We had a Sunday afternoon jazz like gig there. And all the civil rights and freedom riders we called them, would come in and hear us play. And I remember one night after a gig, maybe we finished around twelve or something at night, I took six of the civil rights, you know, members home to my mother’s house. She got up out of her bed, fixed us a full fledged breakfast with biscuits, you know, eggs, bacon, and my mother never complained about anything like that. And Sterling Janice Rose, I don’t know if she’s with us now but she came — she went to Howard University and you know that was the way my mother was. She was a giver. And she always told us it’s better to give than to receive. And she was a domestic worker but she would go and our neighbor Miss Louise and Miss Bertha, they were getting old so she would go by and bathe them and feed them in the morning before she went to work and then after she came back from work she would come back and make sure and feed them and — but we called them home attendants now but she wasn’t even expecting any money or anything, that’s what she did. And we had to do that. And my cousin, the mother of this friend of mine, we called her Congetta, she had the underground railroad system going. Because she lived up near the railroad tracks and all the hobos that came through Jackson knew that they could stop at her house and get a meal. And she would feed them on the back porch but she wouldn’t let them come inside the house. Congetta did that with no pay, you know what I’m saying? And by the knock on the door with her being, “Oh yeah come on in, sit down on the back porch.” And the climate wasn’t like it is now, it was always pretty warm or most of the time. It was just in February and January we may have had to wear coats and it got a little cool down there. It snowed every ten years. But Congetta would do that. That’s the way it worked. Nobody went hungry. There was no homeless people per se, unless they decided they needed to be homeless. We took care of everybody. And everybody looked out for each other. Those who had mental or special needs or all those people, we took care of them too. Everybody knew, okay this person is not [inaudible].
